question: Russia’s two‑year military aggression in Ukraine is not only targeting the population and civilian infrastructure, but also nature. Since 2022, Russia has occupied around 25 % of Ukraine’s protected areas. Ukraine’s ecosystems are constantly suffering from physical and chemical pollution, along with the destruction of natural areas due to the movements of military equipment.

In June 2023, for example, the destruction of the Kakhovka Dam by Russian troops caused an ecological and humanitarian catastrophe, threatening the existence of many species in the aquatic ecosystem. Russia’s intensive and deliberate ecocide is an issue that must be addressed as a matter of urgency. Could the Commission please answer the following questions: 1.
What support is the Commission providing to protect endangered species and habitats in Ukraine?
Would the Commission consider proposing the creation of an international compensation mechanism for damage caused by Russia’s unlawful actions against nature using frozen Russian assets?
answer: The Commission has supported Ukraine in protecting its ecosystems from the environmental damage wrought by Russia’s aggression in multiple ways. The Commission funded a web platform for real-time reporting, redirected funding to allow tracking of environmental damage, providing on-the-ground sampling, and offered its satellite imagery capacities (1).

The Commission supports remediation of environmental damages while ensuring that reconstruction is environmentally sustainable. A significant share of support came under the Phoenix Initiative (2), combining funding and policy advice (3). The EU is an Associate Member of the Register of Damage, the first step of a mechanism for compensation caused by the Russian aggression against Ukraine.

The Commission participated in the High-Level Working Group on the Environmental Consequences of the War, which recently published the ‘Environmental Compact’. It contains policy recommendations on damage assessment, accountability and green recovery and acknowledges the importance of registering information on environmental damages in the Register of Damage.

The Council Conclusions of 18 March 2024 on Green Diplomacy recall the environmental impact of the war in Ukraine, nuclear safety risks and energy and food insecurity. The Conclusions stress the need to assess the damage, to address it in recovery and reconstruction efforts and to hold Russia accountable.

On 20 March 2024, the High Representative and the Commission proposed a Council Decision and a Council Regulation aimed at transferring the profits generated by the management of Russian sovereign assets immobilised in the EU to the Union budget to meet Ukraine’s most pressing needs as well as short-term recovery and long-term reconstruction needs.

Ukraine has made no explicit request to use these capacities so far. https://environment.ec.europa.eu/news/rebuilding-ukraine-2023-02-02_en These include EU programme for the environment and climate action (LIFE) and Horizon Europe project funding, and interventions from the New European Bauhaus expert community to support Ukrainian municipalities in addressing environmental damages.
